notes.meaning: Elihu continues his speech because Job remains silent. Having addressed Job's earlier complaints, he takes the floor again to answer other statements Job has made.
Elihu challenges Job for acting as if his own righteousness were greater than God's. Job had defended his innocence so fiercely that it sounded as though God was treating him unfairly.
Elihu claims Job asked what good it does to live right if innocent people suffer anyway. He accuses Job of talking as though living an obedient life brings no more benefit than sinning.
Elihu offers to answer both Job and the friends who share his line of thinking. He intends to correct their reasoning and explain how God really deals with mankind.
Elihu tells Job to gaze up at the sky and the clouds high overhead. Because the physical heavens are far beyond human reach, the God who made them is infinitely higher and untouched by human actions.
Human wrongdoing cannot harm God or diminish His power. A person's sins break God's law and bring guilt, but they can never injure God's eternal majesty or shake His throne.
Living a good and righteous life gives nothing to God that He lacks. He already owns everything, so human obedience cannot put God in our debt or force Him to reward us.
A person's wickedness or goodness affects only other human beings on earth. Sins harm other people and good deeds help them, but God remains completely above being helped or hurt by what we do.
People cry out under the crushing power of cruel oppressors. Job had pointed to these cries to ask why God seems to let great wrongs go on without stepping in right away.

Elihu explains that the oppressed cry out from sheer pain, but they do not truly seek God their Maker. They fail to turn to the One who can give songs of joy and comfort even in the darkest night of trouble.

God gave human beings reason, making them far wiser than the animals and birds. Animals can only cry out from distress, but people were created with the ability to seek God in faith during hard times.

When sufferers call out and receive no answer, it is because of their own pride. They complain loudly about the cruelty of their enemies, but their own hearts remain stubborn and unhumbled before God.
God does not listen to empty cries that lack sincere faith and humility. Shouting merely out of pain or bitterness is not true prayer, so the Almighty does not answer it.
Elihu warns Job not to lose hope simply because he cannot see God at work right now. Job's situation is fully before God's judgment seat, and Job must wait patiently for Him to act.

Because God does not instantly strike down sinners in anger, people mistakenly assume He ignores foolishness. Elihu points out that God's patience does not mean He is blind to wrongdoing or will leave it unpunished.
Elihu concludes that Job is speaking uselessly and piling up words without true understanding. Instead of waiting quietly before God, Job has spoken rashly in the middle of his grief.
